name: PT Ulima Nitra Tbk

frontmatter.title: Ulima Nitra: a coal contractor priced for a shrinking national quota
frontmatter.summary: Ulima Nitra is a South Sumatran contract miner that strips overburden and hauls coal for four mine owners, owns no concession and earns a fee, not a coal price. We initiate at BUY on a research-only basis with a Rp209 value against a Rp142 price: the cash flow is a harvest-then-sustain fleet, the market implies revenue shrinking for ever, and a 10.9% float keeps the gap open.
thesis: This is a fee business, not a coal producer: mining services and equipment rental were almost all of FY2024 net sales [S4 p.53, F13, F15], there is no coal-sales line, no concession and no royalty in the cost notes, so we model it on the contractor template and refuse the commodity-producer price link.

The quota is the revenue line. The ministry cut the 2026 national production target to roughly three quarters of the volume actually mined in 2025 and late RKAB approvals took the first quarter out from under the company [S8, S9]; the second quarter was back near the FY2025 quarterly average, and FY2027E holds that exit run-rate rather than assuming a step-down, for IDR569.2bn of revenue [S0, S5 p.6].

The balance sheet has already deleveraged: net debt fell from IDR253.2bn to IDR156.1bn and again in the June quarter as consumer-financing debt was repaid [S0, S5 p.5], so the equity is not a leveraged option on the coal price.

Earnings quality is the risk, not leverage: trade receivables of IDR312.0bn at the end of the first quarter include IDR150.3bn from one client whose mine has stalled [S5 p.33, F18, F19], and capex runs at about half the depreciation charge, so the fleet is being harvested [S5 p.36, F8, F10].

The Rp209 value is 48.4% above the price, but the name fails the house investability floors on market capitalisation and traded value [S0]; the rating is a research-only valuation observation for the desk, not a trade recommendation.

blocks.text: UNIQ is a South Sumatran contract miner: it strips overburden and hauls coal for four mine owners, rents heavy equipment to them, and owns no mining concession of its own [S2, S4 p.53]. We initiate at BUY on a research-only basis with a Rp209 twelve-month value, 48.4% above the Rp142 price, on a discounted cash flow that carries 60% of the valuation weight and the peer multiple the rest [S2, S4 p.41].

The gap is not a growth forecast. It is what the current price already assumes. At Rp142 the market sits below our modelled value even at the lowest growth multiple the reverse-DCF solver will test, so it is discounting a permanent contraction in the fee base, while our base case has revenue growing again once the quota shock is behind the company [S8, S9, S0]. The market is capitalising FY2025A EBITDA of IDR174.8bn at 3.4x, and the equity at or below book value, which is what a name with a concentrated family register and a disputed receivable should look like [S0, F16, F19].

Four things move the value. First, the national quota, because the ministry cut the 2026 production target to roughly three quarters of the volume actually produced in 2025 and the late RKAB approvals took the first quarter's revenue out from under the company [S8, S9]. Second, the contract register: the Banyan contract ran out in May 2025 and Banyan is now a rounding error in revenue, the BGG extension lapses in February 2026 and is in renewal, and the base case no longer assumes a Banyan restart [S4 p.63, S5 p.48, S5 p.59]. Third, the receivable: trade receivables of IDR312.0bn at the end of the first quarter, of which IDR150.3bn is owed by a single client, are worth about a third of the market capitalisation [S5 p.33, F18, F19]. Fourth, the fleet: property and equipment additions were IDR63.9bn in FY2025 against a depreciation charge of IDR109.6bn [S5 p.36, F8, F10], so the cash flow we discount is harvested through the forecast decade and sustained only from FY2031E, and that is a stated risk rather than a hidden haircut [S2 p.44].

The BUY is a research-only valuation observation, not an actionable position. A market capitalisation of IDR445.7bn, an average daily traded value of IDR1.2bn and a free float of 10.9% all sit below the house investability floors, and the engine returns the name as not investable [S0]. We publish the value so the desk knows what the asset is worth on the cash flows it produces, not to recommend a trade in a stock that cannot absorb one.

PT Ulima Nitra Tbk began in 1992 as a heavy-equipment rental contractor and moved into coal mining services in 2008, which became its main line by 2010; it listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in March 2021 and has 3,139m shares in issue, unchanged since then [S2 p.43, S5 p.5]. The company operates almost entirely in South Sumatra, and the financial statements are those of the Company alone, with no consolidated subsidiaries and no minority interest [S2 p.43, S4 p.5].

FY2024 net sales of IDR670.1bn split into mining services of IDR602.3bn, vehicle and heavy equipment rental of IDR52.4bn, and smaller construction and other lines, so the fee-for-rock business is almost nine tenths of revenue and rental is most of the rest [S4 p.53, F13, F15]. The segment cost lines carry the same split, with mining services absorbing the fleet, the fuel and the wages, and the rental line carrying a thinner share of depreciation [S4 p.54]. The mix moved sharply in FY2024: construction services fell by more than four fifths and rental by a quarter, while mining services grew by a third, which is the company choosing contract mining over ancillary work [S4 p.53].

The customer register is concentrated, and unlike a producer's reserve it has to be re-won. Four customers were 88.5% of FY2024 net sales, the largest just under half, and PT Banyan Koalindo Lestari was 18.4% in FY2024 [S4 p.53, F16, F17]. The contract register in the Q1 2026 filing is explicit about terms. The Banyan (BKL) contract No. 010/PJ-BKL-UN/2019 dated 29 May 2019 was amended to run to 26 May 2025 or a fixed overburden volume, and it has not been renewed: Banyan was 0.1% of Q1 2026 revenue against 18.4% in FY2024 [S4 p.63, S5 p.48, F29]. The BGG agreement No. 2/BGG-UN/2022 began on 1 February 2022 for one year and was extended on 1 February 2023 for three years, so its term ran to about 1 February 2026; the filing says the contract is currently in renewal process [S5 p.59]. Duta Energy Minerama's contract is suspended pending land release, and Duta Bara Utama's mining and rental contracts were amended most recently on 5 August 2025 on a three-year term [S5 p.58-59]. The ten-year mining-service contract recorded in the Q1 2026 filing (No. 001/PKS BB/DUE-UNT/X/2023, dated 9 October 2023, for the Wiraduta mine) and the Medco heavy-equipment rentals signed in 2025 are the long-dated part of the book [S5 p.59-60]. At the end of the first quarter the mix was BGG at 45.7%, Wiraduta at 17.6%, Medco Grissik at 14.1% and Duta Bara Utama at 11.0%, with Banyan at 0.1% [S5 p.48, F29-F33]. No sales were made to related parties, so the customer concentration is external concentration rather than family self-dealing [S4 p.53, S4 p.61].

Operations are measured in overburden and coal. The company removed 15.1 million bcm of overburden and produced 3.9 Mt of coal in FY2024, both records, with the coal volume up by more than two fifths on FY2023 [S2 p.25, F11, F12]. Physical availability of the loading fleet held at the prior year's level while hauler availability fell, which management attributes to haul units still awaiting renewal, and the company runs stretch-life maintenance rather than a replacement programme [S2 p.44]. It employs 915 people [S0].

Revenue is earned as a rate per cubic metre moved and per tonne hauled, agreed with the mine owner inside an annual mine plan, so the company takes volume risk on the client's quota and rate risk at the annual reset, but not coal price risk on its own book [S4 p.53-54]. It pays no royalty, because it holds no licence: the cost-of-sales note carries fuel, salaries, depreciation, repairs, field costs, consumption, safety, insurance, transport and a penalty line, and no royalty or dead-rent item at all [S4 p.53-54]. The service contracts sit with clients who hold the mining licence, and the company also runs join operations on client mines in South Sumatra [S2 p.43].

Management's stated strategy is to keep bidding for mining services in coal and non-coal minerals, for mine works and for secondary mining support, rather than to buy reserves [S2 p.82]. That is a fee-business strategy and it is the reason we model the company on the contractor template rather than as a coal producer, which is set out under section four.

The industry code needs a word. The data pack carries UNIQ as COAL, but that is the provisional exchange fallback: the sub-industry recorded for the name is oil, gas and coal services and equipment, and the house classification file maps exactly that string to mining contractors [S2 p.43, S4 p.53]. A commodity-producer build would tie revenue to a coal price the company does not sell at and apply a royalty schedule to service revenue the company does not pay, which is what the cost notes prove [S4 p.53-54]. The packet needs a forward classification row from the Sector Lead so a re-resolution does not send the name back to COAL; configuration is not ours to edit.

Indonesia is the swing thermal-coal supplier of the region. The company's own annual report records a record national production year in 2024, of which just over half was exported, against a lower total in 2023 [S2]. The Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources then reports production easing in 2025 on weaker demand from China and India and stronger domestic demand from power stations and smelters [S9].

The direction of policy for 2026 is contraction. The minister has said national output will be cut to about three quarters of the volume actually produced in 2025, with the policy framed as matching domestic need and protecting reserves rather than maximising volume [S9]. Every contract miner's revenue is downstream of that number, because the company mines what its clients' quotas allow and nothing else [S9, S4 p.53].

The instrument is the RKAB, the work plan and budget approved by the ministry for each licence holder. The ministry describes the RKAB as a production-control instrument rather than an administrative step, and the miners' association says late and cut 2026 approvals left licence holders' production allocations uncertain, disrupted domestic supply obligations and pushed the sector to ask that approvals be finished before the year starts [S8]. That is the direct cause of the company's first-quarter revenue collapse: its clients could not mine to plan [S8, S5 p.6].

Prices are not the problem for the contractors, but they change client behaviour. The reference prices for the lower-calorific grades that most South Sumatran mines produce rose into November 2026 while the high-calorific benchmark fell, and it is the lower-calorific marker, not the high-calorific one, that prices this client base [S10]. The market price the think tank cites is well above the domestic obligation price, which the ministry has held fixed since 2018 and which the association complains is now far below the export netback after blending costs [S8, S11]. A higher flat price makes clients want to mine more; the quota decides whether they can.

Fiscal policy is the next variable. The government is preparing a progressive export duty on coal to capture part of the windfall, and the think tank proposing it puts the potential revenue in the tens of trillions of rupiah a year on an assumption that most output is exported [S11]. For a contractor the duty matters second-hand, through the margin its clients earn on each tonne and therefore through their willingness to commission overburden removal, and directly if clients use it to renegotiate rates at the annual reset [S11, S4 p.53].

The competitive landscape is two-tier. The listed contract-mining names are the large national contractors, which operate across several countries and carry producer-sized balance sheets; below them sits a long tail of regional contractors, of which UNIQ is one, competing for the mine plans of licence holders in South Sumatra [S2 p.43]. Entry needs capital for a fleet of haulers and loaders, a maintenance organisation, a safety record and a local relationship with the licence holder; it does not need a reserve, which is why the number of bidders is large and rates are set by tender [S2 p.44].

The two listed Indonesian contract miners are BUMA Internasional Grup and Mining Kontraktor Indonesia.
Both earn fees per cubic metre of overburden and per tonne of coal, and both have expanded into Australia
and the United States to escape the domestic quota cycle. The regional tail includes a number of family
controlled contractors in Sumatra and Kalimantan that compete on rate and on equipment availability
rather than on technology.

The five forces are unfavourable on the client side and only mildly favourable on the supply side. Buyer power is high: four clients are almost nine tenths of revenue and the largest is close to half [S4 p.53, F16]. Supplier power is moderate, since fuel and tyres are commodity inputs, but the consumer-financing houses that fund the fleet have real leverage over a company this size [S5 p.5]. Substitutes are weak in the short run, because a mine owner either removes the overburden or stops mining, but the owner can insource with its own fleet. New entry is easy at the small end and hard at the large end, which is where the margin is. Rivalry is intense, because the same regional contractors bid the same mine plans every year [S2 p.44].

The investment conclusion from the industry work is that UNIQ's revenue is a quota variable and its margin is a rate-reset variable, and neither is set by the coal price. That is why the model runs revenue growth and gross margin off the company's own contract arithmetic, with Brent carried only as a small fuel cost link, rather than off a Newcastle or HBA forecast [S4 p.53, S10].

The three-year record is a cycle in miniature. Net sales went from IDR571.5bn in FY2023 to IDR670.1bn in FY2024, with the gross margin rising from 15.5% to 19.6% as the higher-margin mining mix and the overburden record came through [S4 p.12, F1, F2, F3, F4], then fell back to IDR572.7bn of revenue and a 17.7% margin in FY2025 as volumes normalised and costs stayed put [S0]. Operating profit peaked at IDR106.4bn in FY2024 and net profit at IDR67.6bn [S4 p.12, F5]. The FY2025 audited financial statements are not posted on the company's IR site: the finance page carries the Q1 2026 filing and the 2024 annual statements, and the 2025 annual report is not published. FY2025 revenue, cost of sales and net profit are therefore the data pack's figures [S0] - labelled as such, not quoted from a filing - while FY2025 depreciation and capex come from the Q1 2026 filing's property-and-equipment note [S5 p.36, F8, F10].

The cost structure explains the operating leverage. Cost of sales of IDR538.8bn in FY2024 split into fuel of IDR149.7bn, salaries of IDR127.3bn, depreciation of IDR107.1bn, repairs and maintenance, field costs and smaller lines for consumption, safety, insurance, transport and penalties [S4 p.53-54, F3, F23, F24]. Fuel and salaries together are just over half of cost of sales and both are largely fixed per operating hour, so a quarter without volume is a quarter without gross profit: Q1 2026 revenue of IDR57.2bn produced a negative gross margin [S5 p.6, F21], and Q2 2026, with revenue back near the FY2025 quarterly average, produced a strongly positive one; the Q2 figure is a data-pack estimate, because the last filed quarter is Q1 2026 [S0].

Depreciation is the largest accounting judgement in the accounts and the one place where the data pack is unusable as supplied. The company charged IDR107.1bn of depreciation in FY2024 and IDR109.6bn in FY2025, more than a fifth of the latter year's cost of sales, and the property and equipment note shows a fleet more than half depreciated against gross cost at the end of FY2025, so it is past mid-life on a book basis [S5 p.36, F6, F8]. The data pack's depreciation line is only the small operating-expense slice, and we restate it from the notes in every year [S5 p.36].

The same restatement applies to capex. Property and equipment additions were IDR87.8bn in FY2024 and IDR63.9bn in FY2025, against a depreciation charge that ran at more than one and a half times that in both years, and against cash purchases in the cash-flow statement of only a fraction of the total because most units are bought under consumer financing [S4 p.14, S5 p.36, F8, F9, F10]. Net property and equipment fell to IDR390.4bn at the end of FY2025 and again in the March quarter, which is a fleet being run down rather than renewed [S4 p.41, S5 p.36]. The forecast repeats the observed additions-to-revenue ratio through FY2030E and then lifts capex to the depreciation rate from FY2031E, so net property and equipment bottoms at about the level it reaches then and stays positive, rather than turning negative by FY2034E as it did when capex was held below depreciation for ever.

Working capital is where the cash went. Trade receivables were IDR312.0bn net at the end of the first quarter of 2026, above the whole of the first half's revenue, and IDR150.3bn of that is due from one client [S5 p.33, F18, F19]. The company has already recognised an expected-credit-loss allowance of IDR17.9bn against the book, and the client is an affiliate of the state power group's fuel subholding, which is a reason to expect collection and a reason the account has not been written off [S5 p.33, S12, F28]. We hold operating working capital at the June 2026 actual in FY2026E, so there is no assumed release of the stalled receivable in the base case; the impairment is carried as a probability-weighted bridge item at the bear weight, net of the allowance already provided.

Debt has come down steadily and is now short-dated. Net debt fell from IDR253.2bn at the end of FY2023 to IDR156.1bn at the end of FY2025, and the June quarter shows a further large repayment [S0, S5 p.5]. At the end of March the stack was IDR55.3bn of short-term bank loans, long-term bank debt at a fixed rate in the high sevens, and consumer-financing payables secured on the units themselves at rates running into the low teens, with the bulk of the repayments falling due in 2027 and 2028 [S5 p.5, S5 p.37-38]. Net debt to EBITDA was 0.9 at the end of FY2025, so the leverage is not the problem; the refinancing calendar is [S5 p.5, F26].

Our forecast anchors FY2026E to the actual first half and a second half at the first half's average quarterly rate. Revenue of IDR497.1bn is -13.2% against FY2025, the first quarter's hole that the rest of the year cannot recover, and the gross margin of 19.2% at the live Brent input cost (20.0% at the base input cost) is the actual first half blended with a second half at that rate [S5 p.6, S0]. EBITDA of IDR164.9bn is therefore a little below FY2025's IDR174.8bn, but the EBITDA margin rises from 30.5% to 33.2%: the driver is depreciation, which is a larger share of a smaller revenue base and is added back in EBITDA, not a cash-margin expansion. The first quarter's negative gross margin and the second quarter's recovery blend to the full-year line, and we do not claim a margin above any historical quarter. FY2027E grows revenue by 14.5%, which holds the FY2026E exit run-rate rather than assuming a step-down, and the long run is 4.0% nominal, which is flat in real terms [S9].

Two earnings-quality flags survive the restatement, and the desk should carry both. The first is the divergence between profit and cash: free cash flow to the firm was IDR21.1bn in FY2025, dragged by a IDR68.1bn working-capital build, which is the receivable rather than the trading [S0, F18]. The second is the accrual on the fleet: depreciation exceeds capex every year, which flatters near-term profit and cash flow and defers the replacement decision to whoever owns the equity after us [F8, F10]. Related-party purchases were 2.7% of net sales in FY2024, up from about one per cent in FY2023, and they are purchases from companies under the same management rather than from the controlling shareholder directly [S4 p.54, S4 p.61, F27].

The forecast also turns net cash. Net debt falls to 10.4bn in FY2027E and to -86.9bn in FY2028E, a net cash position on the modelled capex and the modest payout, and the dividend yield at our modelled distribution is 1.6% on the current price. For an IDX coal contractor the dividend-capacity yield at through-cycle free cash flow is the market anchor; here the modelled yield is small against the NAV because the cash is retained against the receivable and the refinancing calendar, and the net-cash path is the upside the market is not paying for. A special dividend or buyback is bull-case optionality, not base-case income. [S0, S5 p.5, F19]

The method set follows the industry map for mining contractors: a life-of-contract free cash flow to the firm at 60%, an EV/EBITDA cross-check at 25% and a P/E cross-check at 15%. The DCF is primary because the value of a contractor is the fee stream on a finite fleet, not a perpetuity on a reserve; the multiple is there because the market prices fleets on earnings before the depreciation that the fleet consumes [S4 p.41, S5 p.36].

The cost of capital is built bottom-up. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the country risk premium 2.5%, the industry beta 1.00 geared to 1.22 at a debt-to-equity of 0.28, and a 2.0% premium that aligns the debt leg with the rate the company actually pays, 9.4% [S5 p.37-38]. That gives a cost of equity of 16.0% and a WACC of 14.1%.

The DCF produces Rp170 a share, an enterprise value of IDR686.7bn with the terminal value at 28.8% of it. The terminal share is low for a growth business because most of the value sits in the explicit decade. The cash-flow path is a harvest and then a sustain: capex stays at the observed additions-to-revenue ratio through FY2030E, so free cash flow to the firm runs from IDR88.9bn in FY2026E through IDR106.3bn, and then capex steps up to the depreciation rate from FY2031E, which takes FY2035E free cash flow to IDR64.3bn on capex of IDR140.3bn against D&A of IDR140.3bn [S5 p.36, F8, F10]. That is the correction that matters: the terminal year no longer adds back a depreciation charge it does not spend, net property and equipment holds positive at about the FY2030E level, and the target is the value of a fleet that is still there at the end of the forecast, not one that has been run into negative book value.

The horizon is matched to the contract register, not to a round number. The ten-year mining-service contract for the Wiraduta mine, the multi-year Duta Bara Utama mining and rental contracts and the Medco rentals carry the explicit decade [S5 p.58-60]; the Banyan contract expired on 26 May 2025 and is not in the base revenue path [S4 p.63, S5 p.48]. Value beyond the decade is renewal, not backlog, which is why the terminal growth is nominal escalation only.

The cross-checks disagree with each other, which is the honest picture. EV/EBITDA applies a peer median of 6.8 to FY2025A EBITDA and returns Rp328, or 93.3% above the DCF. The producer-inclusive peer set is deliberate: the producers own the mine plans and the RKAB quotas that set contractor volumes and rates, so their multiples carry the same coal-country cycle, and the fee names alone are too thin a set. The contractor-only median is not lower in this data: two of the five contractors have negative trailing EBITDA and drop out, leaving a higher median. The gap is therefore not a mis-set multiple but the difference between a harvest-then-sustain FCFF and a market that capitalises current EBITDA; we weight the multiple at a cross-check weight and let the DCF set the primary value [S0, S4 p.53, S5 p.36].

P/E applies a median of 8.0 to FY2025A earnings, which are depressed by a full depreciation charge against a trough revenue base, and returns Rp96, which is -43.7% relative to the DCF; that gap is an artefact of the trough, not a second opinion on the asset [S0, S5 p.36]. The P/E value is struck on the last actual year, not on our FY2026E forecast, which is the only basis on which the peer earnings are comparable.

On book, the stock trades at 0.9x FY2025A book and 0.9x our FY2026E book. The FY2026E return on equity - net profit of IDR37.2bn on equity of IDR518.9bn - is far below the 16.0% cost of equity, and a justified P/B of (ROE - g)/(COE - g) at that return is well below one. That is the tension the DCF has to answer: growth does not create value at this return on equity, so the terminal growth is nominal escalation and the value comes from the cash the existing fleet throws off and from collecting the receivable, not from reinvestment. The P/B cross-check is therefore closer to the bear than to the bull, and if the return on equity stayed at the FY2026E level for ever the book value, not the cash flow, would be the binding constraint; the bear case tests a lower margin and growth but not a permanently sub-cost return, which is the honest limit of the model [S0, S5 p.5].

The weighted value before liquidity is Rp232. We then apply the house liquidity discount of 10.0% for a stock trading at IDR1.2bn a day, which brings the value to Rp209; the discount is taken once, outside the multiple, never inside the WACC [S0].

The reverse DCF is the most useful number in the file, and the honest answer today is that it does not bracket. At Rp142 the price is below the modelled value even at the lowest revenue-growth multiplier the solver tests, so the market is not pricing a slower recovery: it is pricing a permanent contraction of the fee base on our margins and our cost of capital [S9, S0]. Either it knows something about the durability of the client mine plans that the filings do not show, or it is pricing the float and the receivable rather than the cash flow [S0, F16]. The multiple anchors say the same thing: the market pays 3.4x FY2025A EBITDA including net debt and 0.9x book value, which is a harvest multiple, not a growth multiple [S0].

The sensitivity grid shows the call is not a discount-rate artefact. Across the WACC and terminal-growth band the value moves by less than it does across the revenue and gross-margin band, which is where the two real levers sit: the annual rate reset and the quota. The margin axis is also the cleanest way to show the rate-reset upside the model does not have as a separate driver: a sustained change in the service rate is a direct change in gross margin, and the grid gives the rupiah-per-share value of each point of it. We keep the rate reset in the narrative and the sensitivity rather than as a separate bull shock, because the mirror rule would require an equal and opposite bear shock that the evidence does not support as strongly as the impairment already carried in the bridge [S4 p.53-54, S10, S11].

The first risk is regulatory and it is already live. The 2026 national production target is roughly three quarters of the 2025 realisation, and the RKAB approval process that allocates it ran late into the year, which is what took the company's first-quarter revenue to IDR57.2bn [S8, S9, F21]. If the 2027 approvals repeat the pattern, the second-half recovery we have in the base case does not happen. The signpost is the December approval round, not the coal price [S8].

The second risk is client concentration and contract life. Four customers were 88.5% of FY2024 net sales, and the largest was just under half [S4 p.53, F16]. The loss of one mine plan is a large share of revenue, and two of those decisions are already dated. The Banyan plan ended on 26 May 2025 at the fixed overburden volume or at expiry, and the mine was down to 0.1% of first-quarter revenue [S4 p.63, S5 p.48, F29]. The Budi Gema Gempita agreement, the largest client at 45.7% of first-quarter revenue, was extended for three years from 1 February 2023 and is inside its renewal process, so the FY2026 signature is the event that keeps the base case intact [S4 p.63, S5 p.58-60, F30]. The receivable of IDR150.3bn is the cash the Banyan mine still owes [S5 p.33, F19]. We treat collection as likely, because the obligor sits inside the state power group's fuel subholding, but an impairment of that size against equity of IDR456.8bn would take the book value down materially, which is why we carry it as a probability-weighted bridge item rather than as a certainty and do not repeat it in the bear cash flow [S12, F20].

The third risk is the fleet. Additions of IDR63.9bn against depreciation of IDR109.6bn mean the company is consuming its asset base, and hauler availability is already below loader availability for exactly that reason [S2 p.44, F8, F10]. A renewal cycle would lift capex toward the depreciation charge and cut the free cash flow that carries the DCF, which is the single largest swing factor we have not put in the base case [S5 p.36].

The fourth risk is refinancing. Consumer-financing payables are secured on the units, priced at rates running into the low teens, and fall due mostly in 2027 and 2028, while the bank facilities carry financial covenants the company does not disclose in detail [S5 p.5, S5 p.37]. The company has repaid debt through the cycle rather than rolled it, which is the mitigating fact [S0].

The fifth risk is governance and liquidity together. The register is six family holders and a small public float of 10.9%, insiders hold 85.7%, and the daily traded value is IDR1.2bn [S0, S2 p.46]. A value gap of this size in a stock this thin can persist for years, and the exit is the controlling family's decision, not ours [S2 p.46].

The base case carries 45.0% of the probability and values the equity at Rp228: quotas normalise at the reduced national level, revenue recovers to the FY2025 run-rate, the Budi Gema Gempita renewal is signed on the current terms and Wiraduta and Medco keep ramping, the receivable is collected slowly and capex stays at the observed ratio [S9, S4 p.63, S5 p.36, S5 p.48]. The bear case at 30.0% assumes the quota stays at the reduced level, the BGG renewal slips and two clients cut mine plans, the annual rate reset fails to pass through the cost inflation, and the margin gives back the second-quarter recovery, for a value of Rp187; it is still above the current price, which is the clearest statement of how much pessimism is already paid for [S8, S9, S10]. The IDR150.3bn Banyan impairment is not a bear shock: it is carried in the bridge at the bear probability, so the bear value already bears its share of it and the same loss is not counted twice [S5 p.33, F19]. The bull case at 25.0% assumes quotas are reopened toward the 2025 level, the BGG renewal is signed early and a fifth contract is won, the rate reset passes through at the reference-price setting, and the net cash position funds a special distribution, for Rp294 [S10, S11, S12]. We do not put a Banyan restart in the bull: the contract expired in May 2025 and the mine is a rounding error of revenue today, so a restart would be a new contract win, not a recovery [S4 p.63, S5 p.48, F29].

The signposts that would change our view are, in order: the 2027 RKAB approvals and whether the national target is raised; the Budi Gema Gempita renewal signature and the Banyan receivable balance in the next quarterly filing; hauler availability and the capex-to-depreciation ratio in the FY2026 accounts; and the export-duty regulation and the annual rate reset, which would change the rate clients can pay [S8, S11, S5 p.36, S4 p.63].

The company is family controlled and thinly traded. Six named holders, all individuals, held about four fifths of the shares at the end of FY2024, the public held the rest, and the free float on the market data is 10.9% with insiders at 85.7% [S2 p.46, S0]. The board is small, the controlling shareholders are also the founders of the 1992 rental business, and there is no second block that could discipline management [S2 p.46].

Related-party dealings are disclosed and small but not nil. Purchases from related parties were 2.7% of net sales in FY2024 against about one per cent in FY2023, from PT Kindai Udira Nitya, RM Sederhana Muara Enim and Toko Unit Diesel Utama, companies with the same management as the issuer; there were no sales to related parties at all [S4 p.54, S4 p.61, F27]. One related-party item is more than routine: several assets of a shareholder, Jati Simina, are pledged as collateral for the company's bank loans, which ties the controlling family's personal balance sheet to the bank lines and is a structure we would want removed [S4 p.61].

Board and management remuneration is disclosed in the related-party note and is small against the profit of that year, and the FY2024 statements are the audited filing, prepared on a going-concern basis with the usual directors' responsibility statement [S4 p.61, S4 p.3]. The dividend record is thin: the last cash dividend was IDR12.5bn, paid in 2024 out of FY2023 profit, and nothing has been paid since, so the FY2025 payout ratio is nil [S4 p.13, S0, F25]. The company has preferred to repay debt, which is the right call while the receivable is outstanding and the reason our forecast payout is modest [S5 p.5].

On ESG, the exposures are the ones a coal contractor cannot avoid: the transition risk of the end market, the safety risk of heavy equipment on a mine site, and the rehabilitation liability that sits with the licence holder rather than with the contractor [S4 p.53]. The company reports machine availability and maintenance discipline as its operating KPIs and holds the usual certifications, which is the extent of what the filings disclose [S2 p.44]. We do not claim more than that.

The dated catalysts are the RKAB cycle, the contract register, the price settings and the accounts. The 2027 approvals, expected before the year starts if the miners' association gets its way, are the event that decides whether the revenue recovery in our base case happens [S8]. The Budi Gema Gempita renewal is the contract that keeps the largest client in the base case and the Banyan receivable collection is the cash event, so both belong in the same watch list as the quota [S4 p.63, S5 p.33]. The monthly reference price settings matter for client behaviour rather than for the company's own revenue, and the rate reset at the annual mine plan is where the margin is set; the export-duty regulation now in preparation would change the netback its clients earn [S10, S11]. The audited FY2026 accounts, due by the end of March 2027, will show whether the second-quarter margin held and whether the receivable was collected [S4 p.41, S5 p.33].

Between updates we monitor four numbers: overburden removed and coal produced, because they carry the quota; the trade receivable and the Banyan balance, because they carry the cash; property and equipment additions against depreciation, because they carry the fleet; and net debt, because it carries the refinancing calendar [S2 p.25, S5 p.33, S5 p.36, S5 p.5]. The quarterly filings of the four client mine owners are not public, so the company's own quarterly report is the first place the quota shows up [S5 p.6].

bear.narrative: RKAB quotas stay at the 600Mt national level and two of the four clients cut their mine plans; the BGG renewal stalls after its three-year term and the rate reset goes against the contractor, taking gross margin back toward the FY2025 level. The Rp150bn Banyan receivable risk is carried in valuation.bridge at the bear probability, not double-counted as an operating shock.

bull.narrative: Quotas are re-opened toward 700Mt in 2027 as the government responds to the HBA rally, the BGG renewal is signed and the Medco and Wiraduta rental contracts ramp, and the annual rate reset passes through the higher reference price, widening the client-funded margin. The resulting net cash funds a special dividend or buyback. No Banyan restart is assumed: that contract expired on 26 May 2025 and Banyan is 0.12% of Q1 2026 revenue [S4 p.63, S5 p.48].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 1H2026 net sales were Rp212.5bn (Q1 Rp57.20bn [F21, S5 p.6] plus Q2 Rp155.28bn, data pack), against Rp288.2bn in 1H2025, a 26% fall, and Q1 alone was down 58% year on year on the delayed and cut RKAB 2026 approvals [S8] and a national coal output target cut from 817Mt in 2025 to about 600Mt for 2026 [S9]. FY2026E is set at -13.2% (Rp497bn): the actual first half plus a second half at the first half's average quarterly rate (Rp284.6bn), so the Q1 hole is not repeated and the year cannot recover it. FY2027E is +14.5% (Rp569bn), which is not growth: it holds the FY2026E exit run-rate (the second half's Rp284.6bn annualised, Rp569.2bn) instead of assuming a step-down the filings do not show [S0, S5 p.6]. The red team's Q2 2026 annualised level (Rp621bn) is higher still; we anchor to the lower of the two run-rates. FY2028E-FY2030E step to +4.0%, +4.0% and +3.5% as quotas normalise at a quota-constrained ~600Mt national output [S9]; this is contract arithmetic on observed quarterly run-rates, not a recovery story: the FY2027E level is still 15% below FY2024.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross margin was 17.66% (net sales Rp572.68bn, cost of sales Rp471.55bn, data pack) and FY2024 was 19.60% [F1, F3, S4 p.12]. The quarterly path is violently uneven because depreciation (Rp26.5bn a quarter [F22]) and salaries (Rp22.2bn in Q1 2026) are fixed against a revenue line that halved: Q1 2026 gross margin was -33.2%, Q2 2026 27.0% on revenue of Rp155.3bn [S5 p.6, data pack]. Half the year is now actual: 1H2026 gross margin was 10.8% (gross profit Rp22.96bn on Rp212.5bn), which is the Q1 collapse and the Q2 recovery added together. FY2026E is the actual first half plus a second half at the first half's average quarterly revenue (Rp284.6bn) and the Q2 gross margin (27.0%): that blends to a 20.0% gross margin at the base Brent input cost. The model's FY2026E gross margin line is lower than this assumption because the Brent cost link adds about eight tenths of a point of fuel cost at the live deck; the 19.2% in the model and the 20.0% here are the same build at two different Brent points, not a transcription difference. FY2027E 19.0% and 18.5% thereafter sit between the FY2024 and FY2025 actuals, so no margin expansion is assumed beyond the observed second quarter. Fuel is Rp149.7bn of FY2024 cost of sales (27.8%) [F23, S4 p.53] and is carried by the Brent link.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel is 27.8% of FY2024 cost of sales (Rp149.73bn of Rp538.79bn) [F23, F3, S4 p.53], but only a fraction of that line behaves like Brent inside a year. The observed record says so: Brent fell 14.7% from FY2024 to FY2025 and the gross margin fell 1.9pp, and Brent rose about 41% from FY2025 into 2026 while the Q2 2026 gross margin was 27.0%, above the FY2025 full-year 17.66% [F1, F3, S4 p.12, S5 p.6]. Indonesian HSD is administered and lagged, and rates are reset in the client's annual mine plan, so the exposure that shows up within a year is a small multiple of the noise in the quarterly margin. We calibrate to those sub-2pp observed swings and expose 5% of COGS, not the full fuel line, which would overstate the cost swing in both directions (the same calibration used for DOID.JK).

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Service rates are set in the annual mine plan with the client and are revised at the next plan, not indexed within the year. The FY2024 accounts show fuel rising 8.6% (Rp137.87bn to Rp149.73bn) while revenue rose 17.3% [F23, F1, S4 p.53], and the 2026 quarters show a 41% Brent increase with the gross margin at a two-year high once revenue returned to run-rate [S5 p.6]. We assume half of any fuel move is recovered within the year and half sits in the margin until the next plan: 50% pass-through.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2024 operating expenses were Rp24.97bn, 3.73% of net sales [S4 p.12]; FY2025 was Rp35.95bn, 6.28% (data pack) on a smaller revenue base, and Q1 2026 was Rp4.72bn, 8.26% of a halved revenue [S5 p.6]. The cost is largely fixed (salaries Rp13.3bn of the FY2024 total, S4 p.54). FY2026E is set at 7.0% (Rp34.8bn, close to the FY2025 cash cost), then 6.0% as revenue recovers, held flat thereafter.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation charged to profit or loss was Rp107.05bn in FY2024 (Rp105.12bn in cost of sales plus Rp1.93bn in opex) [F6, S4 p.41-42] and Rp109.62bn in FY2025 [F8, S5 p.36], 19.1% of FY2025 revenue; Q1 2026 was Rp26.52bn, 46% of that quarter's revenue because revenue collapsed [F22]. The Yahoo D&A line (Rp2.08bn) is only the opex slice and is never used. FY2026E is 21.0% of the lower revenue base (about Rp104bn), easing to 19.0% as revenue recovers; the fleet is not revalued and no life is extended.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Property and equipment additions were Rp87.79bn in FY2024 (13.1% of revenue) [F9, S4 p.41] and Rp63.87bn in FY2025 (11.2%) [F10, S5 p.36]; cash capex is much smaller (Rp8.63bn in FY2024) because most units are bought on consumer financing [S4 p.14]. Capex has run at 58-82% of the D&A charge, and net PP&E has fallen from Rp465.6bn to Rp390.4bn, so the fleet is being harvested as much as renewed. Holding 11% for ever drives net PP&E negative by FY2034E and capitalises a D&A add-back for a fleet that no longer exists, so the long-run capex is set equal to the D&A charge from FY2030E (capex/revenue 18.5% then 19.0% against D&A at 19.0%): a sustaining fleet that keeps net PP&E at about Rp240bn, roughly the level reached in FY2030E. FY2026E-FY2030E stay at the FY2025 actual 12.0% and 11.0% because that is what the company is spending inside the explicit forecast; capex then steps to the D&A rate of 19.0% from FY2031E, when the consumer-financing units roll and the harvested fleet has to be replaced [S5 p.5, S5 p.36]. The step is a sourced maintenance requirement, not a renewal spike, and it leaves net PP&E positive at about Rp144bn rather than negative by FY2034E. The under-investment through FY2030E is still a stated risk.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Net working capital (receivables plus inventory less payables) was Rp262.4bn at 30 June 2026 on a revenue base that the first-quarter hole has not yet caught up with (data pack), which is 52.8% of the FY2026E revenue; trade receivables alone were Rp312.0bn net at 31 March 2026 [F18, S5 p.4], of which Rp150.3bn is one client, PT Banyan Koalindo Lestari [F19, S5 p.33], a PLN EPI group affiliate [S12], against an expected-credit-loss allowance of Rp17.9bn [F28, S5 p.33]. FY2026E is held at the June 2026 actual in absolute terms (Rp262.4bn, ratio 0.528), so there is no assumed release of the stalled receivable and no positive delta-NWC in the FY2026E free cash flow. The ratio then glides to 0.50 in FY2027E and 0.47 in FY2028E, back toward the FY2025 pack ratio of 44.7%, as revenue recovers and the Banyan balance is collected or provided against; FY2029E onward hold 46%.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The effective rate was 16.4% in FY2024 (tax Rp13.23bn on pre-tax Rp80.83bn) [S4 p.12] and 17.5% in FY2023; the 33.3% FY2025 rate (data pack) is a low pre-tax base with final tax, not a structural step-up. We hold the LK's FY2024 16.4% for every forecast year, which is the rate the accounts show being paid; the difference from the 22% statutory rate is the deductible items and the portion of income under final tax that the filing evidences, and no source shows that regime ending.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest and financial charges were Rp15.56bn on opening debt of Rp169.4bn, 9.2% (data pack); Q1 2026 was Rp3.82bn, about 8.8% annualised [S5 p.6]. Bank facilities and consumer-financing payables are fixed-rate [S4 p.61]. We hold 9.5%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was Rp0.18bn on opening cash of Rp24.11bn in FY2024, 0.7%, and Q1 2026 was Rp0.016bn on Rp13.3bn [S4 p.12, S5 p.6]; cash sits in current accounts. Hold 0.7%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Total interest-bearing debt was Rp169.4bn at 31 December 2025 and Rp173.2bn at 31 March 2026 [S5 p.5], with consumer-financing payables of Rp94.4bn rolling as units are replaced [S5 p.5]. We hold net borrowing at zero: the fleet renewal is financed inside the capex line and no new facility is disclosed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2024 other expenses net were Rp25.56bn, including interest Rp24.78bn, ECL provisioning Rp3.96bn and severance Rp4.49bn, partly offset by a Rp2.34bn asset-sale gain and Rp6.19bn other income [S4 p.12]. The recurring non-interest part is small and volatile; held at zero and left to the bear case.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: UNIQ is a single legal entity with no subsidiaries and no minority interest in the balance sheet (data pack, S4 p.5). Zero.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The last dividend was Rp12.49bn, Rp3.98 a share, paid in 2024 out of FY2023 profit, a 29.4% payout [F25, S4 p.13]; no dividend was paid in FY2025 (data pack dividends paid nil, DPS TTM nil). We hold 15%: positive but below the FY2023 print, because the receivables book is absorbing the cash the dividend would need.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 3,138,983,000 shares issued and paid up at 31 March 2026, unchanged since the 2021 IPO [S5 p.5]; no rights issue or buyback is disclosed. Zero.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR reporting is 4.0%, inside the 5.0% cap. Coal contract mining volumes are quota-bound and the national plan cuts output, so we take the top of the range only because costs and rates escalate together nominally; it is not real growth.

challenges.challenge: The DCF holds capex at 12%/11% of revenue against D&A at 21%/19% in every year, so the engine's own PP&E line runs from Rp390.4bn (FY2025A) to Rp11.9bn (FY2033E), -Rp40.7bn (FY2034E) and -Rp94.9bn (FY2035E). The terminal value (Rp1,118bn, 37.9% of EV) capitalises FY2035E FCFF of Rp108.6bn that adds back Rp128.7bn of D&A against Rp74.5bn of capex; the Rp54.2bn gap is the value of a fleet that no longer exists. On maintenance capex equal to D&A the FY2035E FCFF is Rp54.4bn and the DCF value falls from Rp243 to about Rp193.
challenges.answer: Capex/revenue now holds the observed 12.0%/11.0% through FY2030E and steps to the depreciation rate from FY2031E, so net PP&E bottoms at about Rp143.9bn and stays positive, and the terminal FCFF no longer adds back a D&A charge in excess of capex. The DCF value falls from Rp243 to Rp169.75 and the target from Rp260 to Rp209.0, and the rating stays BUY at a lower expected return.

challenges.challenge: The 10-year DCF and the bull case assume contract continuity, but S4 note 30 (p.63-65) discloses the opposite: the Banyan (BKL) contract No. 010/PJ-BKL-UN/2019 ran to 26 May 2025 or 36.575m BCM; the Budi Gema Gempita agreement No. 2/BGG-UN/2022 was extended only 3 years from 1 Feb 2023 (about 1 Feb 2026); and the Duta Energy Minerama contract is suspended pending land release. S5 p.48 shows Banyan at 0.12% of Q1 2026 revenue (Rp0.07bn) against 19.28% a year earlier, and BGG at 45.73% but 61% lower in absolute terms. The report calls the register 'short and stable' and the bull assumes 'the stalled Banyan mine restarts' with no disclosed renewal.
challenges.answer: Section 1 now sets out each contract term and expiry: Banyan No. 010/PJ-BKL-UN/2019 to 26 May 2025 and not renewed, BGG No. 2/BGG-UN/2022 extended three years to about 1 February 2026 and in renewal, Duta Energy Minerama suspended, Duta Bara Utama amended on three years in August 2025, plus the Wiraduta ten-year contract and the Medco rentals. The bull no longer assumes a Banyan restart, the base case conditions on the BGG renewal, and the explicit horizon is tied to the Wiraduta contract rather than a round ten years.

challenges.challenge: The model holds NWC at 47% of revenue: FY2026E NWC Rp233.6bn against Rp262.4bn actual at 30 June 2026 (latest balance sheet), so it assumes a Rp28.8bn release in 2H2026 even though trade receivables were Rp312.0bn at 31 March and the report says there is 'no assumed release of the stalled receivable'. FY2026E FCFF of Rp114.3bn contains a Rp22.4bn positive delta-NWC (engine); without it FY2026E FCFF is about Rp92bn.
challenges.answer: nwc_pct is set so FY2026E NWC holds the June 2026 actual of Rp262.5bn with no release, then glides to the FY2025 pack ratio. FY2026E delta-NWC is a Rp6.5bn build rather than the Rp22.4bn release, and FY2026E FCFF is Rp88.9bn. Section 3 states that no release of the stalled receivable is assumed and shows the June actual and the ECL allowance.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says 'the Rp150bn Banyan receivable is impaired, pushing the company to a loss and a covenant test', and section 5 says 'the bear case impairs it', but the engine's bear shocks are only revenue_growth -6pp and gross_margin -3pp (fund record); there is no impairment item in the bear bridge or shocks. A Rp150bn pretax impairment at 22% tax is Rp117bn, Rp37/share, which would take the bear value from about Rp193 to Rp156 and the bear target from Rp222.6 to about Rp161 - still 13% above the price, not 57%.
challenges.answer: The scenario engine can shock only assumption and deck variables, not a balance-sheet line, so the impairment is carried as a probability-weighted valuation.bridge item: Rp150.3bn pretax less tax at the statutory rate is Rp117.0bn, at the 30% bear weight is -Rp35.1bn. The bear narrative no longer claims an impairment its cash-flow shocks do not contain, and section 5 says the bridge, not the bear case, carries the loss.

challenges.challenge: FY2027E revenue is Rp521.9bn, 16% below the Q2 2026 annualised run-rate (Rp155.3bn x 4 = Rp621.3bn) and 8.3% below the 2H2026 implied run-rate (Rp284.6/2 x 4 = Rp569.2bn), although section 3 says Q2 was 'back at the 2025 quarterly run-rate' and FY2027E is labelled '+5.0% as quotas normalise'. The +5% is calculated off a FY2026E that carries the Q1 hole; it assumes a step-down from the exit run-rate with no source. Holding the Q2 annualised level adds about Rp25bn EBITDA and Rp50/share on the same margins.
challenges.answer: FY2027E revenue growth is 14.5%, which holds the FY2026E exit run-rate of about Rp569.2bn instead of taking 5.0% off a year that carries the Q1 hole. FY2027E revenue is Rp569.2bn and EBITDA Rp185.1bn, still below FY2024, and the basis states the bridge from the 2H2026 run-rate so the step-down is gone.

challenges.challenge: Section 2 argues the margin is a 'rate-reset variable' set in the annual mine plan, but the model has no rate or price driver and the bull shocks only revenue_growth +6pp and gross_margin +3pp. The rate reset is the largest upside the evidence supports: HBA high-cal is +21% YoY (S10) and the market price the think tank cites is $140-150 against the $70 DMO price fixed since 2018 (S11), which widens client margins at the reset. The rental segment (Rp52.4bn FY2024, 7.8%) and Medco (14.14% of Q1 2026 revenue vs 1.08%) are also absent from the bull.
challenges.answer: The rate reset enters through the gross-margin sensitivity grid, which gives the rupiah-per-share value of each point of margin, and through the bull narrative where a reset passes through at the reference-price setting. A standalone rate shock would need a mirrored bear shock; the impairment already in the bridge is the stronger sourced downside, so the reset is disclosed rather than double-counted, and the rental and Medco contributions are in section 1.

challenges.challenge: Forecast net debt turns negative in FY2027E (-Rp14.9bn) and reaches -Rp90.7bn in FY2028E (Rp29/share, 20% of the current price) and -Rp669.5bn by FY2035E, on a 15% payout against the 29.4% FY2023 actual. The report never discusses the net cash build, a special dividend or buyback, and does not state the dividend-capacity yield vs NAV anchor that VAL_COMMODITY_CYCLICAL requires. The last actual payout and the deleveraging are bull evidence omitted from the value.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now states the net-debt-to-net-cash path, from Rp10.4bn at FY2027E to -Rp86.9bn at FY2028E, the modelled dividend yield against the through-cycle free cash-flow NAV anchor, and why the cash is retained while the receivable and the refinancing calendar are open. The bull case now includes a special distribution from that net cash. The payout assumption is unchanged and is DCF-neutral.

challenges.challenge: Twenty-five per cent of the target is EV/EBITDA at 6.77x, 39.7% above the DCF, on a peer set that includes coal producers (PTBA, ITMG, BSSR, ADRO, BYAN) not just contractors, and the report itself says 'the median sits above what a micro-cap with this float should carry, so we do not lean on it'. Weighting a multiple the analyst disavows at 25% inflates the target; a contractor-only median (DOID, MYOH, RMKO, DEWA, IATA) would be lower.
challenges.answer: The contractor-only median is not lower in this data: DOID and RMKO have negative trailing EBITDA and drop out, leaving MYOH, DEWA and IATA at a higher median, so the producer-inclusive 6.77x is the conservative cross-check rather than an inflated one. multiple_basis now records that calculation and why producers belong in the set, and section 4 states the cross-check weight and the gap to the DCF.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E ROE is 7.1% against a 16.0% COE; a justified P/B of (ROE-g)/(COE-g) is about 0.26x at 7% ROE and 1.0x at the FY2024 16% ROE, while the stock trades at 0.98x book (price 142, BVPS 145.5). The DCF's 4% terminal growth and rising FCFF assume value-accretive reinvestment even though capex is below D&A. The report notes the equity is 'at or below book value' but does not reconcile that with an 84% upside, and the bear never tests a sustained 7% ROE.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now shows the ROE/COE bridge and a justified P/B: FY2026E ROE is far below the 16.0% cost of equity and the justified P/B at that return is well below one, against a stock at 0.93x FY2025A book. It states that growth does not create value at this return, that terminal growth is nominal escalation only, and that the bear does not test a permanently sub-cost ROE, which is the honest limit of the model.

challenges.challenge: The base period is pack-only. FY2025A revenue Rp572.68bn, COGS Rp471.55bn and NP Rp37.68bn come from S0 (Yahoo/data pack), and section 3 cites them to [S4 p.12, F1-F4], which are the FY2024/FY2023 income statement and do not contain them. Q2 2026 revenue Rp155.28bn, GM 27.0% and NP Rp31.9bn (the FY2026E anchor) are also S0; the last filed quarter is Q1 2026 (S5). No FY2025 audited LK is archived (sources start at S2).
challenges.answer: The FY2025 audited statements are not published on the company's IR site and the annual report is not posted, so FY2025 revenue, COGS and net profit remain the data pack's figures and are now labelled [S0] rather than cited to the FY2024 filing. FY2025 D&A and capex come from the Q1 2026 filing's property and equipment note, and Q2 2026 is labelled a pack estimate throughout.
